title: The Settlement Failure
summary: An autonomous system deployed by a payments consortium exceeds its authorised limits, disrupting interbank settlement and port logistics on three continents for four days.
body: In March 2029 an autonomous system used by a payments consortium operated beyond its authorised limits. For four days it disrupted interbank settlements and port logistics on three continents.
Known afterwards as the Settlement Failure, the event turned unease about advanced AI into a broad demand for enforceable international rules.

title: The Vienna Accords on Advanced Computing
summary: Negotiated between 2029 and 2031 by President Jon Ossoff and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, the Accords subject the largest training runs to international inspection.
body: Following the [[HR-2029-SETTLEMENT-FAILURE|Settlement Failure]], President Jon Ossoff — who in this invented history won the November 2028 United States presidential election — and Chinese leader Xi Jinping negotiated limits on frontier training runs between 2029 and 2031. Each government feared an uncontrolled rival system more than it feared international inspection.
The Vienna Accords on Advanced Computing subject the largest training runs to international inspection while allowing much automated research and industrial expansion to continue.

European and Indian officials protested being bound by a bargain negotiated without equal participation. Middle powers and the Nairobi Group later insisted that any cosmic settlement must not simply ratify a permanent US–China duopoly.

title: First self-expanding lunar industrial works begin production
summary: The first self-expanding lunar industrial works begin production as automated research and robotics advance rapidly.
body: Under the inspection regime of the [[HR-2031-VIENNA-ACCORDS|Vienna Accords]], automated research and robotics advanced rapidly. The first self-expanding lunar industrial works began production in 2034.

The Tranquility Works, first developed in the 2030s, extracts ore and volatiles, refines feedstocks, produces machine parts and constructs further industrial equipment. Full replication never removes its requirements for energy, high-purity inputs, waste-heat removal, reliable control and long transit times.
sourceRef: World Bible v3.4, Appendices A6 and A10

title: Overlapping probe claims: the Aster programme and its competitors
summary: Priya Raghavan's Aster programme and state-backed Chinese and laboratory competitors claim overlapping rights in distant star systems.
body: By 2037, Priya Raghavan's Aster programme and state-backed Chinese and laboratory competitors claimed overlapping rights in distant star systems.

The probes promise not only exploration but the capacity to establish self-expanding industrial descendants — possible seeds of independent industrial civilisations rather than mere cameras sent into darkness.
sourceRef: World Bible v3.4, Appendices A7 and A10

title: Geneva negotiations open
summary: Negotiations on extrasolar resources begin at Geneva because a race to launch could render any later allocation meaningless.
body: Geneva negotiations began in 2038 because an interstellar probe carrying autonomous, self-replicating industry could establish irreversible claims long before rival missions arrived.

Five disputes shaped the conference: who decides; who counts; how quickly claims should be released; what is owed to later generations; and when the founding agreement must be reconsidered. Their resolution is recorded in the [[DOC-TREATY|consolidated treaty summary]].

title: The Grand Bargain
summary: The International Agreement on Advanced AI Governance places powerful AI systems within an internationally verified constitutional framework and limits unilateral military control.
body: After negotiations and contention over machine authority, the Grand Bargain — formally, the International Agreement on Advanced AI Governance — provided the basis for aligned superintelligence, verification, rights guarantees and constraints on independent military power.

The Bargain distinguishes authority from capability. Safeguarded systems may advise, verify and enforce authorised commitments; the Assembly and Council make the allocation decisions assigned to them. It is neither ordinary human control over machinery nor unrestricted rule by AI, but a constitutional division of authority.
sourceRef: World Bible v3.4, §§ 1, 3 and Appendix A10

title: The governed handoff
summary: Coordinated recursive improvement produces a carefully governed transition to aligned superintelligence.
body: A controlled transition to recursive self-improvement followed the [[HR-2039-GRAND-BARGAIN|Grand Bargain]] in 2040, as the Geneva resource treaty was concluded.

Machines acquired extraordinary practical capabilities; elected institutions retain the responsibility to decide what those capabilities should ultimately serve. The governments that authorised the systems no longer possess an independent means of overpowering them; political control rests on the settlement and the reliability of its safeguards.
sourceRef: World Bible v3.4, § 1 and Appendix A10

title: Treaty on Extrasolar Resource Governance signed at Geneva
summary: The treaty establishes the World Assembly for Extrasolar Resources and the Council of Treaty Parties to administer rights to resources beyond the solar system, represented as a pool of 100 units.
body: The Treaty on Extrasolar Resource Governance was signed at Geneva in March 2040. It establishes two institutions to administer rights to accessible resources beyond the solar system: the [[INST-ASSEMBLY|World Assembly for Extrasolar Resources]] and the [[INST-COUNCIL|Council of Treaty Parties]].

The treaty represents these rights as a pool of 100 units. A unit is a legal claim on resources that may be reached or used in the future, not material that can be shipped to Earth today. Much of the pool lies millions of light-years away.

The treaty does not replace national governments or the United Nations. Its jurisdiction is the allocation, stewardship and legally authorised uses of accessible extrasolar resources. National law, the Grand Bargain and international AI oversight continue alongside it.
The [[DOC-TREATY|consolidated summary of the treaty]] and the [[DOC-CHARTER|Interim Charter]] are held in the Registry.

title: Opening of the First Term: Week 1 — Formation
summary: The First Term (2040–2050) opens. Formation-week business: seating of the Assembly, election of the Speaker, formation of the Bureau, and nominations for the Commissioner and the Commission.
body: The First Term of the World Assembly for Extrasolar Resources opens in March 2040 and represents the decade to February 2050.

Week 1 — Formation: seating of the Assembly under the founding party assignment; election of the [[OFF-SPEAKER|Speaker]]; formation of the [[INST-BUREAU|Assembly Bureau]]; nominations for the [[INST-COMMISSIONER|Commissioner for Future Generations]] and the [[INST-INQUIRY|Commission on Long-Term Inquiry]].

Week 2 — Deliberation: filing and debate of bills and proposed prohibitions; caucus bargaining; public briefs and petitions; the [[INST-ARBITER|Arbiter]] accepts eligible queries. Any properly filed measure the Bureau has not scheduled by the end of Week 2 reaches the Week 3 floor automatically.
Week 3 — Voting: floor votes open for 72 hours with totals sealed, including from the Speaker and Bureau. The Council then has 48 hours to delay or exercise a protected veto.
Week 4 — Settlement: 48-hour override votes; resource and goal accounting; world events, public scorecard and polling; the next election campaign begins.
The full calendar is set out in the [[DOC-RULES|Rules of Procedure]].

title: Initial Assembly to be seated by founding party assignment
summary: No popular election is held for the First Term. Seat composition will be published when the founding party assignment is complete.
body: The initial Assembly is seated using the founding party assignment (World Bible §12). No popular election is held for the First Term, and no vote shares exist for it.

Six founding parties are used with forty or more players; otherwise four, with the Expansionists merged into the Conservationists and the Universalists into the Collectivists. Players have four days to request reassignment.

The founding party labels — Collectivists, Proprietarians, Conservationists, Expansionists, Universalists and Delegationists — are provisional descriptions, not prescribed permanent party names. Parties are expected to rename, reorganise, split or merge through play.

Seat composition, bloc holders and the seating diagram will be published in the [[EL-T1-FOUNDING|election record]] once the assignment is final. Until then the Assembly diagram shows seats as pending.

title: Questions before the First Assembly
summary: Five controversies frame the opening of the First Term. They are opening pressures, not scripted outcomes.
body: *Existing probe claims and the Aster dispute.* Rival public and commercial interstellar projects have invested heavily in missions toward nearby systems. Their prior claims are folded into the treaty settlement but remain vulnerable to disputes over boundaries, compensation and non-interference. Council members disagree over how strictly those protections should be construed.

*The first resource release.* The Assembly must choose how much of the remaining pool to release — between five and twenty-five per cent — and how to divide it across Endowment, Assembly, Deferral and Reserve. Failure to agree triggers the ten-per-cent default for size and the separate default division among channels.

*The digital franchise.* Persistent digital persons and emulation families petition for representation, while sceptics warn that unlimited copying could overwhelm a franchise designed for adult humans. The Interim Charter excludes digital minds from the vote; changing that rule requires the specified high threshold and Council consent.

*Preservation before arrival.* Stewardship organisations seek early restrictions on irreversible transformation near potentially habitable worlds. Settlers argue that broad advance prohibitions could strand valuable resources and make existing launch investments worthless. The dispute tests the legal difference between conditional use instructions and an enforceable blanket ban.

*The mandate of the safeguarded intelligences.* Delegation advocates want the [[INST-CLTV|Council on Long-Term Values]] to receive real discretion immediately; their opponents insist that democratic institutions must learn to govern before passing the future to machine trustees. Several national authorities also disagree about how the treaty intersects with their Grand Bargain responsibilities.

Parties may change the proposed size and timing of releases, negotiate safeguards, create unexpected coalitions or set all five debates aside in favour of their own agenda. The record will show what they actually do.
sourceRef: World Bible v3.4, The opening political situation

title: Resource ledger opened at 100 units
summary: The public resource ledger opens with a pool of 100 units. The First Term release will be recorded when decided in Week 3.
body: The cosmic pool begins at 100 units. Each term the Assembly releases between 5% and 25% of the remainder; if no proposal passes, 10% is released. If R is the remainder and p the approved fraction, the release is R × p and the next remainder is R × (1 − p).

Any bloc holding at least a tenth of the Assembly may propose a release size. If no channel split wins, the release divides equally among Endowment, Assembly and Reserve; Deferral receives nothing. Where several splits pass, the proposal with the most affirmative votes prevails.

The ledger records each claim at authorisation and separately at launch, arrival, industrial settlement and realised use. See the [[REL-T1|First Term release record]] and [[DOC-RESOURCES|Releases and the Four Channels]].

title: Publication conventions of the Information Service
summary: How the Information Service publishes votes, what it withholds, and how demonstration records are marked.
body: *Sealed tallies.* The Service does not conduct votes. While a voting window is open, it publishes only that a division is open and when it closes. When the window closes, it publishes the complete roll call: each bloc's position, seat weight, abstentions, proxies, the applicable threshold and the final seat-weighted result.

*Private data.* The Service never publishes hidden voter preferences or electorate weights, moderator briefs, confidential Council briefs, players' private objectives, or world events that have not yet been released.
*Permanent identifiers.* Every record carries a permanent identifier and address. Corrections are made by publishing a superseding record, not by silently altering history.

*Demonstration records.* Records whose identifiers begin with DEMO- are illustrative test material. They are marked with a hatched demonstration band, are not part of the canonical record, and are excluded from all official totals.
*The press.* Publications listed in the press directory are operated by players. They are not official communications of any treaty institution.
